questions.question: Let (P) be $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ and (D) its dual $\min\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$. Which statement is the strong duality theorem for this pair of linear programs?
options: (P) has a feasible solution if and only if (D) has one, and then the two optimal values are equal.
If (P) and (D) both have optimal solutions, then the optimal value of (P) is at most that of (D).
(P) has an optimal solution if and only if (D) has one, and then the two optimal values are equal.
(P) has an optimal solution if and only if (D) has one, and then the optimal value of (D) is $-\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$.

questions.question: Let (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ and its dual (D) $\min\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$. Suppose (D) has no optimal solution. What does strong duality say about (P)?
options: (P) has no optimal solution either, so it is infeasible or unbounded.
(P) is infeasible, since a program without optimum has an infeasible dual.
(P) is unbounded, since (D) then gives no upper bound on its values.
Nothing, since the theorem assumes an optimal solution of (P).

questions.question: Let (P) be $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ and (D) its dual $\min\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$. Suppose it is known only that (P) has a feasible solution. Which statement about (D) is correct?
options: (D) has an optimal solution whose value equals the largest value of (P).
(D) may have no feasible solution at all, because (P) may be unbounded.
(D) has a feasible solution, but its objective may be unbounded below.
(D) has a feasible solution, because the dual of a feasible linear program is always feasible.

questions.question: For (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ and its dual (D) $\min\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$, (P) has exactly one optimal solution $\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$. Which statement about (D) is correct?
options: (D) has exactly one optimal solution as well, since the dual of (D) is (P).
(D) has infinitely many optimal solutions, since its feasible region is unbounded.
(D) has an optimal solution of value $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$, which need not be unique.
(D) has an optimal solution, but its value can exceed $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$.

questions.question: The linear program $\max 3x_1+5x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq7$, $x_1+2x_2\leq12$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ has the optimal solution $\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}=(2,5)$. What is the optimal value of its dual $\min 7y_1+12y_2$ subject to $y_1+y_2\geq3$, $y_1+2y_2\geq5$, $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$?

For (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ and its dual (D) $\min\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$, (P) has optimal value $24$; (D) has a feasible point $\boldsymbol{y}$ of value $27$. What follows?
options: $\boldsymbol{y}$ is optimal for (D), since every value of (D) is at least $24$.
Strong duality fails for this pair, since $27$ differs from $24$.
The optimal value of (P) must be $27$, so the value $24$ was computed wrongly.
$\boldsymbol{y}$ is not optimal for (D), whose optimal value is $24$.

questions.question: A firm makes products 1 and 2 with profits $30$ and $20$ per unit, subject to machine hours $2x_1+x_2\leq100$ and labour hours $x_1+x_2\leq80$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$; its optimal plan is $\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}=(20,60)$. A buyer offers prices $y_1,y_2\geq0$ per hour with $2y_1+y_2\geq30$, $y_1+y_2\geq20$. What is the smallest possible total offer $100y_1+80y_2$?

Find the optimal value of $\min 12y_1+5y_2+10y_3$ subject to $3y_1+y_2+2y_3\geq4$, $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, which is the dual of the one-variable linear program $\max 4x$ subject to $3x\leq12$, $x\leq5$, $2x\leq10$, $x\geq0$.

To prove strong duality for (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ with Farkas' lemma, one takes an optimal solution $\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$ of (P) and some $\varepsilon>0$. Which system of inequalities is shown to have no solution $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, and why?
options: $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}^{{\ast}}+\varepsilon$, since a solution would beat the optimum.
$\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}^{{\ast}}$, since $\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$ has the largest value.
$\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{b}$, since an optimal solution makes every constraint tight.
$\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}^{{\ast}}-\varepsilon$, since values below the optimum are excluded.

questions.question: In the Farkas proof of strong duality for (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$, with $\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$ optimal and $\varepsilon>0$, the variant of Farkas' lemma gives $(\boldsymbol{u},z)\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ with $\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{u}\geq z\boldsymbol{c}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{u}<z(\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}+\varepsilon)$. Why is $z=0$ impossible?
options: Then $\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{u}\geq z\boldsymbol{c}$ fails, because $\boldsymbol{c}$ has at least one positive entry.
Farkas' lemma always returns a nonzero vector $(\boldsymbol{u},z)$, so its last entry $z$ must be positive.
Since $\varepsilon>0$, the bound $z(\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}+\varepsilon)$ is positive for every $z\geq0$.
Then $(\boldsymbol{u},0)$ meets the same conditions for $\varepsilon=0$, so that system has no solution, yet $\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$ solves it.

questions.question: For (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ and its dual (D) $\min\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$, assume it is proved that if (P) has an optimal solution, so does (D), with equal value. How does the converse follow?
options: From weak duality alone: $\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}^{{\ast}}$ bounds every value of (P), so this bound is attained.
Rewrite (D) in the form of (P); its dual is (P), and the proved direction applies.
It needs the extra assumption that (P) is feasible, which the dual cannot guarantee.
It does not follow: (D) can have an optimal solution while (P) is unbounded.

questions.question: The linear program $\max 3x_1+2x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq5$, $x_1+3x_2\leq9$, $x_1\leq4$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ has the optimal solution $(4,1)$. Its dual is $\min 5y_1+9y_2+4y_3$ subject to $y_1+y_2+y_3\geq3$, $y_1+3y_2\geq2$, $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$. Which $\boldsymbol{y}$ is optimal for the dual?
options: $\boldsymbol{y}=(3,0,0)$
$\boldsymbol{y}=(1,1,0)$
$\boldsymbol{y}=(2,0,1)$
$\boldsymbol{y}=(0,1,1)$

questions.question: The linear program (P) $\max 4x_1+2x_2+5x_3$ subject to $x_1+x_2+2x_3\leq8$, $2x_1+x_2+x_3\leq10$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ has dual (D) $\min 8y_1+10y_2$ subject to $y_1+2y_2\geq4$, $y_1+y_2\geq2$, $2y_1+y_2\geq5$, $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, whose feasible corner points are $(4,0)$, $(2,1)$, $(0,5)$. What is the optimal value of (P)?

For a real number $s$, let (P) be $\max sx_1+x_2$ subject to $-x_1+x_2\leq1$, $x_2\leq3$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, with dual (D) $\min y_1+3y_2$ subject to $-y_1\geq s$, $y_1+y_2\geq1$, $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$. For which $s$ does (P) have an optimal solution, and what is the optimal value of (D) at $s=-\tfrac{1}{2}$?
options: $s<0$; at $s=-\tfrac{1}{2}$ the value is $2$
$s\leq0$; at $s=-\tfrac{1}{2}$ the value is $1$
$s\leq0$; at $s=-\tfrac{1}{2}$ the value is $3$
$s\leq0$; at $s=-\tfrac{1}{2}$ the value is $2$

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{A}$ be a square matrix with $\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}=-\boldsymbol{A}$, and suppose the linear program (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq-\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ has an optimal solution, with optimal value $v$. What can be said about $v$?
options: Any real number: strong duality relates (P) to its dual, not to a fixed number.
$v=0$: the dual has the feasible region of (P) and the value $-v$, and strong duality gives $v=-v$.
$v\leq0$, and $v<0$ is possible: weak duality gives $v\leq-v$, but no more.
$v\geq0$, and $v>0$ is possible: $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}$ is feasible with value $0$.

questions.question: For (P) $\max\{\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}\colon\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b},\ \boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$ and its dual (D) $\min\{\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\colon\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{c},\ \boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}\}$, the Farkas proof of strong duality gives, for each $\varepsilon>0$, a feasible $\boldsymbol{y}$ of (D) with $\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}<\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}+\varepsilon$, where $\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$ is optimal for (P). Which fact guarantees that (D) has an optimal solution?
options: A feasible linear program with bounded objective has an optimal solution, and $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$ bounds (D) below.
The feasible region of (D) is compact, so the continuous objective $\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}$ attains its minimum.
Taking $\varepsilon=0$, Farkas' lemma gives $\boldsymbol{y}$ with $\boldsymbol{b}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}\leq\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$ directly.
Values approaching $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}^{\ast}$ from above force the minimum to be attained.

questions.question: For a parameter $t\geq0$, let (P) be $\max 2x_1+x_2+4x_3$ subject to $x_1+x_2+x_3\leq t$, $x_2+2x_3\leq6$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, with dual (D) $\min ty_1+6y_2$ subject to $y_1\geq2$, $y_1+y_2\geq1$, $y_1+2y_2\geq4$, $\boldsymbol{y}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$. Which formula gives the optimal value of (P) for every $t\geq0$?

(P) $\max 2x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq4$, $x_1\leq3$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ has optimal solution $(3,1)$ with value $7$. In the Farkas proof of strong duality with $\varepsilon=1$, one needs $(u_1,u_2,z)\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ with $u_1+u_2\geq2z$, $u_1\geq z$ and $4u_1+3u_2<8z$. Which triple works?
